newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives scrap as leadership battle looms.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives scrap as leadership battle looms.

text.p: Britain's enfeebled opposition Conservatives sparred over Europe on Thursday as the party's 164 MPs puzzled over the best way to elect a successor to party leader John Major.

Conservative infighting over the extent of Britain's future ties with the European Union was blamed as one reason for their dreadful showing in the May 1 election, when they lost power after 18 years in office.
EU commissioner Sir Leon Brittan warned the party not to "seek in vain to regain popularity by adopting the anti-European approach again".

"A lurch to the right spells disaster and further electoral defeat for anything up to a generation," Brittan said in remarks he was due to deliver in London on Friday. "The Conservative Party should not and need not tear itself apart on the issue of Europe.
"The last election showed that the Eurosceptic stance was not exactly a winning streak, to put it mildly."
He said the only way back for a party that has governed Britain for all but 17 years since World War Two was to re-occupy the centre ground.

But one of the leadership contenders, John Redwood, like Brittan a former cabinet minister, said Conservatives must "awaken our country from its slumbers" in which power was drifting from London to Brussels.
He said there would be little point in future British elections if foreign and defence policies were decided collectively at EU level.
Redwood is regarded as the most Eurosceptic among the six former ministers running for Major's job even before the rules for the contest, expected to take place next month, have been decided.

Conservative legislators were to meet at 1600 GMT to discuss whether to continue with the previous practice -- under which MPs alone vote for a leader -- or to bow to demands from the rank-and-file for a say in the decision.

But the election on Wednesday night of right-winger Sir Archie Hamilton as chairman of the 1922 Committee of backbench MPs which formally runs the election process led to speculation that the status quo will not be disturbed.
In a further sign of the unhappy state of the party, some contenders for the leadership are now openly questioning Major's stewardship.
"All too many in our party have had their loyalties stretched, often to breaking point, in recent years. I want all those Conservatives to come back home," said Redwood.
Redwood resigned from Major's cabinet in 1995 to unsuccessfully challenge him for the leadership on a right-wing platform.
William Hague, a former Welsh Secretary who is now seen as the front-runner in the leadership stakes, also appeared to censure his former boss.

Speaking on Wednesday night, Hague appeared to accuse Major of indecisiveness when he said: "One of the lessons of the past few years is that it is easier to unite the party behind a clear position than a constantly shifting fudge."
